2026 U.S. Senate elections

Forecasts from synthetic (LLM) voters first, and from state-level regression second

Author

Yi Zhi Zhang

Published

October 31, 2026

Silicon sampling

Silicon sampling asks large language models to play survey respondents (Argyle et al. 2023). Each synthetic voter is a persona built from a real respondent of the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES): age, gender, race, education, income, party identification, ideology and so on. We describe the persona to a model, tell it the 2026 Senate race in the persona’s state, and ask how the persona will vote. Many personas, several models and five repeats each give a synthetic electorate, which is weighted to the real one. Synthetic samples can be biased in ways real polls are not (Bisbee et al. 2024), so a 2024 backtest against the real results is used to calibrate every forecast below.

This is the project’s main approach. The conventional regression forecast follows in the second part of this page.

NoteReal LLM results

Everything in this part comes from stored model replies (5,173 personas in 35 states, three models) collected on 30 to 31 October 2026 and processed by scripts/04-forecast.py; this page re-reads the saved files and queries no model.

The forecast is the share of the vote a Republican receives against the main opposition (a Democrat, or an independent in Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota), taken from 10,000 simulated elections. Republicans are favoured in 21 of the 35 races and keep control of the Senate in 72% of simulations. The shaded cards and the map below name the candidate of the favoured side.

Do the models agree?

The three models land close together. Only GPT-4o mini and Llama 3.3 70B were backtested on 2024 (their knowledge ends before that election), so only they feed the headline; DeepSeek V4 Flash has no backtest and is shown for comparison.

How the forecast is built

Personas

Personas are real 2024 CES respondents (scripts/02-build_personas.py), at most 150 per state, written up in the first person. The sample is built from 2024 respondents even for 2026, so it describes the 2024 electorate, not 2026 voters.

Asking the models

Each reply is one call to a model with this system prompt and persona-plus-question prompt (an illustration; no model is called here):

You will be given a description of a person. Answer from this person's perspective, using only knowledge about politics that they would have.

I am a 67-year-old Hispanic woman living in Texas. I have some college education but no degree. My family income is between $80,000 and $100,000 a year. In politics, I consider myself a strong Democrat. I would describe my political views as moderate. I never attend religious services. I follow what's going on in government and public affairs hardly at all.

It is November 2026. In this year's midterm U.S. Senate election in Texas, the main candidates are a Republican and a Democrat. I will vote for ...

Reply with exactly one of: Republican, Democrat, Other, Would not vote. No other text.

The wording follows Bisbee et al. (2024): answer as the person, using only what they would know. Every persona is asked five times per model at temperature 1.0, so a persona’s answer is a distribution, not a single vote. Pure independents mostly answer “Other”, so they are asked a second, forced-choice question that allows only the Republican or the main opponent, as in survey follow-ups for undecided voters.

From answers to votes

  1. Persona share. For each persona and model, the Republican share is Republican answers divided by answers for any major candidate actually on the ballot (Republican, Democrat or independent). Pure independents use their forced-choice answers.
  2. Weights. Each persona counts as its CES survey weight times its chance of voting: validated turnout for 2024, and turnout rates by age group, college and news interest estimated from CES 2022 for the 2026 midterm.
  3. State estimate. The weighted mean of persona shares, with a bootstrap standard error.

Calibration and uncertainty

Raw synthetic shares are not forecasts. For each backtested model a line is fitted to the 33 races of 2024 (GPT-4o mini: actual = 0.19 + 0.65 × estimate; Llama 3.3 70B: actual = 0.21 + 0.62 × estimate), which pulls the estimates toward the middle and shifts them toward Republicans. The 2026 estimates are passed through that line. Uncertainty then comes from five sources in 10,000 simulated elections: a national swing shared by all states (standard deviation 3 points, an assumption, because one election cannot measure it), a state-level error (standard deviation 4.7 points, measured by leaving each 2024 race out in turn), the model used, and sampling error in the synthetic voters.

The synthetic voters follow party identification almost perfectly: strong and leaning partisans vote their party in nearly every reply. The answers that move the forecast come from independents, whose Republican share is between 40% and 55% depending on the model.

Internal validation: the 2024 backtest

The same pipeline was run on 2024, when the answer is known: 4,833 personas in the 33 states with a Senate race.

Model Bias (pp, actual minus model) Mean absolute error (pp) Winners called
GPT-4o mini 1.6 5.7 28 of 33
Llama 3.3 70B 3.3 6.4 28 of 33

Reading. Person by person, the synthetic voters agree with the real vote 91% of the time, slightly below a party-line baseline that simply has everyone vote with their side (95%); that baseline cannot predict independents, who are where the models help and where they are weakest. At the state level the raw estimates are too Democratic (the bias column) and too spread out (calibration slopes near 0.6), which is why calibration is needed. After it, the models still miss by about six points on average and call 28 of 33 winners.

Do silicon sampling and regression agree?

The two approaches name the same winner in 31 of 35 races. They differ in:

State Silicon sampling Regression P(Republican wins), silicon (%) Regression: Democratic two-party share (%)
FL Republican Democratic 73.7 54.4
GA Opposition Republican 33.4 46.5
MT Opposition Republican 31.0 43.8
NC Republican Democratic 54.3 52.6

Silicon sampling is calibrated on a single election (2024), while the regression is validated against certified results from six cycles; the second part of this page documents the regression and its accuracy.

Discussion and caveats

  • Synthetic is not a poll. The “voters” are 2024 respondents described to a model; no one answered a 2026 survey.
  • Calibration rests on one election. The line that corrects the models is fitted to 33 races in 2024, and a midterm may differ.
  • Some uncertainty is assumed, not measured. The 3-point national swing is a judgement, and the seats-not-up count is taken from the forecast script.
  • Candidates are described by party, not name. The model cannot know who the nominees are, so the favoured candidate is the nominee of the favoured side.
  • Independents are the hard part. Models agree with real independents about two thirds of the time in 2024, and four races have an independent challenger.
  • Models differ in knowledge. The backtested models have older knowledge cutoffs than DeepSeek V4 Flash, which has no backtest.

Regression forecast: the second approach

A conventional alternative uses no language model. It regresses each state’s past Senate vote on its demographics and partisanship, using certified results from 2014 to 2024, and predicts 2026 from the 2024 profiles. The rest of this page documents that approach; its results are unchanged from the earlier version of this site.

NoteReal data

Features come from the Cooperative Election Study (CES, 2014-2024) and the Census ACS 5-year estimates. Targets are CES pre-election Senate intent; accuracy is also checked against certified results from the MIT Election Lab. No 2026 survey exists, so 2026 features carry the 2024 profiles forward.

Summary

  • Coverage: 35 of 35 Senate races have a predicted Democratic, Republican and Undecided share; the three shares sum to 100% in every state (checked).
  • Model: ridge regression on log-ratios of the three shares, using state demographics and party identification (features: ces+acs), trained on 2014, 2014+2016+2018, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2022+2024, 2024, all, midterms.
  • Predicted winners (model trained on all): 14 Democratic, 21 Republican.
  • Who wins: every race below names the nominee of the predicted-winning party, with the percentages, in a card per state and on a map.
  • Vote counts: Senate seats are decided by statewide popular vote, so a state’s vote share is the right quantity to predict; there is no Electoral College.

Race-by-race forecast

One card per race. The bar shows the predicted Democratic (blue) and Republican (red) share of the two-party vote; the predicted winner’s portrait is larger. Below the bar, the three-way shares include the undecided. Official portraits exist only for people who serve or have served in Congress; other nominees show initials. Idaho, Nebraska and South Dakota have no Democratic nominee on the ballot (independents are the main challengers), so a predicted Democratic share there means the generic Democratic vote.

Accuracy

Two tests are reported, both with features lagged by two years (the 2024 survey predicts 2026, so the 2022 survey predicts 2024, and so on):

  • Forward-chaining is the honest forecast test: train on earlier cycles only, predict the next one.
  • Leave-one-state-out holds out a state but keeps the other states of the same election in training. It is optimistic, because those states reveal that year’s national swing; it is shown for comparison.

The baseline predicts every state with the training-set average share, computed inside each training fold.

Data

  • data/01-raw_data/ces_2014_2020.parquet, ces_2022_2024.parquet: CES respondents (Harvard Dataverse).
  • data/01-raw_data/acs_state.parquet: ACS 5-year state demographics (Census API).
  • data/01-raw_data/senate_results.csv: certified statewide Senate returns, 2014-2024 (MIT Election Lab).
  • data/02-analysis_data/regression_*.parquet: model metrics and the 2026 forecast.

How independents and special races are coded

  • Independents who caucus with a party are coded by that party in the certified results: Angus King (Maine) and Bernie Sanders (Vermont) count as Democrats. The CES Senate question already places them in its Democratic slot. Independents who do not caucus with a party (such as Dan Osborn in Nebraska 2024) stay in other.
  • Special and regular races are treated alike. A race counts if, after that coding, it has both a Democratic and a Republican candidate; a state with two such races in one year (for example Georgia 2020) pools their votes. Nebraska 2024’s regular race (Fischer v. Osborn) has no Democrat, so only its special race (Ricketts v. Love) counts.

Leakage audit

A forecast may only use what was known before the election. I checked every step of the pipeline for information that would not have been available, and fixed what I found.

Issue What could leak Fix
Same-year features Features and targets came from the same survey year and the same respondents; for 2026 we only have 2024 data. Features are now lagged two years (cycle y uses the survey of y - 2); same-year tables are kept only to measure the leak.
ACS vintage The ACS 5-year estimate for year Y is published after the year-Y election. Lagged with the other features, so only data published before the election are used.
Same-cycle information Leave-one-state-out let other states’ results from the same election (the national swing) inform the held-out state. Kept, labelled optimistic. The headline test is forward-chaining on earlier cycles.
Time travel Leave-one-cycle-out and predict-other-years let later cycles train a model that scored earlier ones. Removed.
Baseline fold The mean-share baseline was computed on all training rows, including the held-out state. Computed inside each fold.
2026 forecast Models trained on same-year features were applied to two-year-old features. The forecast now uses models trained on lagged features.

Checked and clean: certified results are never used to fit a model (only to score it, or as a baseline’s earlier result); ridge penalty and feature scaling are fit inside each training set; every baseline uses only results from years strictly before the target year. One residual: CES case_ids do not repeat across cycles in the cumulative file, so any panel overlap between survey waves cannot be checked.

How much did the leak flatter accuracy? The figure compares lagged (honest) with same-year (leaky) features.

Simple baselines

Before trusting a regression, compare it with predictions that need no fitting at all. Ideas considered:

  1. Party-ID majority (pid3): the party with more self-identified voters in the state wins.
  2. Party-ID majority with leaners (pid7): the same, but leaners count for their party.
  3. Last Senate result: the state’s most recent certified Senate winner (persistence).
  4. Last presidential result: the state’s most recent presidential winner.
  5. Majority class: every state goes to the party that won most earlier races.
  6. Mean share: every state gets the average two-party share of earlier races.

All six use only information from before the target election, and are scored on exactly the same state-races as the regression (those where every method makes a prediction), against certified results.

Reading. On identical rows the best regression (ridge direct two-party, all earlier cycles (ces)) calls 89% of winners correctly; the best simple baseline, last presidential result, calls 91%. The regression does not beat the best baseline at calling winners. The lowest vote-share error is last presidential result at 4.0 points. The regression’s distinct value is the full three-way share forecast, including Undecided.

Previous results as features

The two baselines that did best, the last presidential and last Senate results, are known before the election, so they can also be features. Two feature sets add them: prior (previous results only, no survey) and ces+prior (survey profile plus previous results). Each state’s last presidential and Senate share come from a year strictly before the target election; where a state had no earlier Senate race, the presidential share is used and a flag marks it.

How the headline model was chosen

The headline forecast is not picked by looking at the final results. It is chosen the standard way: by validation performance, then reported on a holdout cycle that played no part in the choice.

  • Candidates: four feature sets (ces, ces+acs, prior, ces+prior) crossed with three training windows (all earlier cycles, the last two, the last one): 12 models. By project decision the headline trains on all six cycles, so only the four all candidates are eligible to be chosen; the other windows are shown for reference.
  • Validation: each candidate predicts 2018, 2020 and 2022, trained only on earlier cycles (forward-chaining). The winner among the eligible candidates is the one with the lowest error in the Democratic two-party share against certified results (winner accuracy breaks ties).
  • Holdout: 2024, the most recent cycle, is predicted by every candidate for transparency but never used to choose.

Chosen: ces+acs trained on all earlier cycles (the all set for 2026). On the untouched 2024 holdout it has an error of 5.6 points and calls 88% of winners. The holdout’s own best candidate was prior (last 2) at 2.7 points; that is expected, because validation picks the best candidate on average, not the best on one cycle. With only three validation cycles and about 33 races each, differences of a point or so between candidates are within noise, so averaging several good models would be a reasonable next step.

Direct two-party model

The main model predicts the survey’s three-way split and then reads off the two-party share. A second model predicts the certified Democratic share of the two-party vote directly: a ridge regression on its logit, fit on earlier cycles’ real results, using the same features. It cannot say anything about Undecided, but it targets the quantity that decides the race.

On the same forward-chaining test (all cycles, lagged features) the direct model is a little more accurate than the three-way model with survey-only features and about equal once previous results are included. For 2026 with ces+acs features it differs from the headline by 1.9 points on average and calls 2 of 35 races differently.

Midterm-only models

Midterm electorates differ from presidential-year ones, so a second family of models is fit on midterm cycles only (2014, 2018, 2022) and used to predict 2026. They are compared with the all-cycle models on the same later midterms: 2018 is predicted from 2014, and 2022 from 2014 and 2018. The all-cycle models may use every earlier cycle, including presidential years.

It trains on only one or two cycles, so it has far less data, and the presidential-year cycles evidently still help. For 2026 the two models call 0 of 35 races differently.

Method

  1. Unit of analysis: one row per state per election cycle.
  2. Features (lagged two years): survey-weighted state profile (share male, white, Black, Hispanic, college-educated, mean age, Republican and Democratic party identification), ACS demographics when available, and a midterm-year indicator.
  3. Targets: weighted Democratic, Republican and Undecided/other shares of Senate vote intent, which sum to one. A multi-class regression is fit on additive log-ratios, so predictions stay positive and sum to one.
  4. Penalty: ridge, chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation.
  5. 2026 features: no 2026 survey exists, so the 2024 profiles are carried forward.
  6. Candidate characteristics are not modelled. A search found no open dataset covering candidates’ race, gender and incumbency for both major-party Senate candidates across 2014-2024 (the FEC flags incumbency but not race or gender; Ballotpedia and OpenSecrets are not open). The 2026 nominee names, incumbency and portraits on this page are used for display only, not as model inputs.

Run the whole pipeline with uv run scripts/05-regression.py and rebuild the figures with uv run scripts/06-make_figures.py.

Caveats

  • Targets are survey intent, not votes; “Undecided” includes Not Sure, No One and third-party answers.
  • State profiles come from survey samples; small states have few respondents.
  • Party-identification features come from the same respondents as the targets.
  • No candidate-level model inputs (race, gender, incumbency, quality, spending; no open dataset) and no uncertainty intervals yet.
  • Independents who caucus with a party (e.g. Maine, Vermont) are coded by party label.

The full list is in caveats.txt in the repository.
